question: In Philemon 1:1-2, alongside Philemon and the church in his house, who else are explicitly named as recipients in Paul's salutation?
opt1: Beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier
correct: Beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier
explanation: Paul addresses his personal appeal to Philemon, including Apphia (likely Philemon's wife), Archippus (a Christian minister designated as fellowsoldier), and the local assembly meeting in Philemon's home. Philemon 1:1-2 (KJV) - "Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer, And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house:"

question: According to Philemon 1:4-5, what virtues of Philemon prompted Paul to thank God and make mention of him always in his prayers?
opt1: Hearing of thy political influence and honors in the Roman provincial court
opt2: Hearing of thy love and faith, which thou hast toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all saints
opt3: Hearing of thy strict enforcement of Mosaic legal penalties against runaways
opt4: Hearing of thy commercial wealth amassed through shipping across Greece
correct: Hearing of thy love and faith, which thou hast toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all saints
explanation: Paul's continuous thanksgiving is inspired by reports of Philemon's steadfast faith in Jesus and his generous love demonstrated toward all the saints. Philemon 1:4-5 (KJV) - "I thank my God, making mention of thee always in my prayers, Hearing of thy love and faith, which thou hast toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all saints;"

question: In Philemon 1:7, why does Paul experience great joy and consolation in Philemon's brotherly love?
opt1: Because Philemon purchased physical weapons for the defense of the church
opt2: Because Philemon paid the legal bail to release Paul from Roman prison
opt3: Because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother
opt4: Because Philemon constructed a magnificent stone basilica in Colosse
correct: Because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother
explanation: Philemon's practical benevolence brought profound comfort to Paul, as needy believers repeatedly experienced deep refreshment through his hospitality. Philemon 1:7 (KJV) - "For we have great joy and consolation in thy love, because the bowels of the saints are refreshed by thee, brother."

question: According to Philemon 1:8-9, on what basis does Paul choose to make his appeal, rather than commanding with apostolic authority?
opt1: For imperial law's sake I issue a binding mandate, being a Roman citizen entitled to civil immunity
opt2: For Mosaic covenant's sake I demand strict obedience, being an authorized Pharisaic rabbi
opt3: For church canon's sake I impose an ecclesiastical decree, being an ordained high priest
opt4: For love's sake I rather beseech thee, being such an one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ
correct: For love's sake I rather beseech thee, being such an one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ
explanation: Rather than exercising apostolic authority to compel obedience, Paul tenderly appeals on the basis of Christian love as an aged ambassador and prisoner for Christ. Philemon 1:8-9 (KJV) - "Wherefore, though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient, Yet for love's sake I rather beseech thee, being such an one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ."

question: In Philemon 1:10, for whom does Paul passionately intercede, and how does he describe their spiritual relationship?
opt1: For my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds
opt2: For my fellowprisoner Aristarchus, who shared my Roman dungeon cell
opt3: For my courier Tychicus, whom I commissioned to deliver sacred scrolls
opt4: For my physician Luke, who tended my bodily infirmities in prison
correct: For my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds
explanation: Paul pleads for the runaway bondservant Onesimus, affectionately calling him his spiritual child fathered to faith while chained in prison. Philemon 1:10 (KJV) - "I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds:"

question: In Philemon 1:11, what play on words does Paul make regarding the name Onesimus (which means 'useful' or 'profitable')?
opt1: Which in time past was a free craftsman, but now is enslaved to Roman debtors
opt2: Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me
opt3: Which in time past was a Greek philosopher, but now is a silent ascetic in prayer
opt4: Which in time past was a violent rebel, but now is an armed soldier in the legions
correct: Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me
explanation: Paul makes a poignant pun on Onesimus' name: once useless and unprofitable as a runaway slave, he has been transformed by grace into someone deeply profitable to both master and apostle. Philemon 1:11 (KJV) - "Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me:"

question: According to Philemon 1:15-16, how does Paul interpret Onesimus' temporary departure in light of divine providence, and in what new relationship must Philemon receive him?
opt1: That thou shouldest punish him with physical stripes; not as a brother, but as a treacherous fugitive
opt2: That thou shouldest sell him immediately in the Roman market; not as a household slave, but as common merchandise
opt3: That thou shouldest receive him for ever; not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved
opt4: That thou shouldest banish him into the wilderness; not as a Christian believer, but as an excommunicated stranger
correct: That thou shouldest receive him for ever; not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved
explanation: Paul illuminates God's overarching providence: Onesimus' brief flight led to eternal redemption, so that he returns transformed into a beloved brother in Christ. Philemon 1:15-16 (KJV) - "For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever; Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord?"

question: What beautiful picture of substitution and imputation does Paul provide in Philemon 1:17-18?
opt1: If thou count me an apostle, demand payment from the church treasury; if he stole goods, let Caesar judge him
opt2: If thou respect my bonds, forgive half his debt; if he caused damage, compel him to work double hours
opt3: If thou desirest my blessing, sell his inheritance; if he owes anything, seize his family as surety
opt4: If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself. If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account
correct: If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself. If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account
explanation: Paul acts as an earthly mediator mirroring Christ: he asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus as Paul himself, assuming full personal liability for any financial debt or wrong. Philemon 1:17-18 (KJV) - "If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself. If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account;"

question: In Philemon 1:19, what legal guarantee does Paul write with his own hand, while subtly reminding Philemon of a greater spiritual debt?
opt1: I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides
opt2: I Paul have signed an imperial promissory bond under Roman civil law: albeit thou owest money to the Ephesian elders
opt3: I Paul have sealed this scroll with the ring of the Jerusalem apostles: albeit thou hast never supported my missionary journeys
opt4: I Paul have recorded this oath before the high court of Achaia: albeit thou owest taxes to the governor of Asia
correct: I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides
explanation: Paul writes a personal binding promissory note to repay any loss, while gently reminding Philemon that he owes his very spiritual life and salvation to Paul's ministry. Philemon 1:19 (KJV) - "I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides."

question: According to Philemon 1:23-24, who sends salutations as Paul's 'fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus', and who are named as his fellowlabourers?
opt1: Silvanus, my fellowprisoner; Titus, Timothy, Tychicus, Apollos, my fellowlabourers
opt2: Epaphras, my fellowprisoner; Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers
opt3: Alexander, my fellowprisoner; Hymenaeus, Philetus, Hermogenes, Carpus, my fellowlabourers
opt4: Erastus, my fellowprisoner; Trophimus, Zenas, Artemas, Aquila, my fellowlabourers
correct: Epaphras, my fellowprisoner; Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers
explanation: Paul conveys greetings from Epaphras, his companion in Roman imprisonment, along with his inner missionary circle: Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke. Philemon 1:23-24 (KJV) - "There salute thee Epaphras, my fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus; Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers."
